The intended implementation style is deliberately evidence-oriented.
MadLava MUST report observable facts, their source, and their accuracy.
It MUST NOT turn correlation into automatic causality, constructors into total allocation counts, or Throwable construction into a fabricated application-failure count.
The words **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **REQUIRED**, **SHOULD**, **SHOULD NOT**, and **MAY** have their usual RFC-style meanings.
Internal code MAY use lower-level terms such as aggregator, sampler, transformer, event source, or reporter, but the public configuration and output vocabulary MUST use `features`.
one distributable JAR;

a full observability backend;

a heap analyser such as Eclipse MAT;
the Spark UI or History Server.
OpenJ9 tracing operates inside the JVM and can observe VM-native trace points.
MadLava uses the standard Java Instrumentation API and observes selected Java behaviour by transforming bytecode and injecting minimal callbacks.
MadLava MUST remain portable across supported HotSpot-compatible Java 11, 17, and 21 runtimes.
Spark is the primary troubleshooting use case, but the generic core MUST remain independent from Spark.
MadLava MUST help identify where to investigate next.
It MUST NOT claim to prove root cause automatically.
`madlava-agent-0.1.0.jar` — the single JVM agent artifact;

**Production safety**
agent failures MUST NOT terminate or corrupt the target application;
feature failures MUST be isolated;
the reporter MUST NOT block application threads.
**Low default overhead**
polling features MAY be enabled by default;
bytecode-heavy, stack-heavy, allocation-heavy, or dump-heavy features MUST be disabled by default;
no transformer MUST be registered if no enabled feature requires bytecode instrumentation.
**Explainability**
output MUST indicate accuracy, availability, sampling, truncation, and degradation;
generated insights MUST explain their evidence.
**Bounded resource usage**
maps, queues, stacks, samples, files, and retained details MUST be bounded;
overload MUST trigger throttling or dropping, never unbounded growth.
**Generic JVM use**
all non-Spark features MUST operate without Spark on the classpath.
**Deep Spark driver visibility**
the Spark feature MUST observe driver-side structures and correlate them with JVM behaviour;
it MUST not depend on `spark.plugins`.
**Usable reports**
output MUST be machine-readable without another backend;
the repository MUST include an offline visual viewer with timelines, rankings, collapsible detail and raw inspection;
viewer warnings MUST surface sampling, dropped keys, truncation, partial coverage and feature degradation.
**Open-source professionalism**

This distinction is mandatory because one Throwable instance may be created without being thrown, thrown multiple times, caught internally, wrapped, or propagated to the driver.
**Creation tracking**
instrument successful completion of selected `Throwable` constructors;
count one created instance after the outermost constructor completes;
include exceptions created and caught internally.
**Explicit throw tracking**
instrument `ATHROW` bytecode instructions in selected application, Spark, serializer, parser and Py4J classes;
record the concrete Throwable class and sampled throw site;
deduplicate nested instrumentation callbacks for the same throw operation.
**JFR exception events**
when enabled and available, consume `jdk.JavaExceptionThrow` and `jdk.JavaErrorThrow` events;
use JFR as the preferred source for implicit JVM throws that do not correspond to an instrumented `ATHROW` instruction;
declare source and coverage explicitly.
**Propagation observations**
method-profiling exceptional exits MAY record that a Throwable propagated through a method;
propagation MUST NOT be counted as a new throw unless the source confirms a new throw event.

This section is normative.
The report vocabulary MUST prevent technically correct counters from being interpreted as stronger claims than the probes support.
MadLava reports observed footprints.
It MUST NOT automatically conclude that the largest metric is the root cause.
Generated insights MAY say:
“This method accumulated the most observed time.”
“Throwable construction increased during the same interval.”
“A large collect action coincided with driver heap growth.”
They MUST NOT say:
“This method caused the incident” without a separately justified causal experiment;
“The application failed N times” when only constructors were observed;
“This object is exactly N bytes” when only a stream or buffer delta was available.
The report viewer MUST present automatic conclusions as **insights**, **suspicions**, or **suggested experiments**, never as unquestionable root-cause verdicts.
nested method time remains part of the caller duration;
blocking, GC pauses and scheduler delay during the invocation remain part of elapsed time;
cumulative duration across concurrent threads may exceed application wall-clock duration;
`totalDurationNanos` answers how much elapsed work accumulated, not how much the method extended the critical path;
a high count may be more important than a high average, or it may merely be noisy;
interval deltas are required to identify bursts that cumulative totals hide.

`completedCount`;
`normalExitCount`;
`exceptionalExitCount`;
`unfinishedCount = startedCount - completedCount`, with weakly consistent snapshot semantics;
total/min/max/average duration for completed observations.

`explicitThrowCount`: selected observed `ATHROW` operations;
`jfrThrowCount`: JVM/JFR exception events, when available;
`thrownCount`: total according to the explicitly declared throw sources;
`propagatedExitCount`: method invocations that completed exceptionally because a Throwable escaped;
`caughtInternallyEstimate`: optional inference, always labelled `ESTIMATED`.

Then OpenAI Build Week arrived: the perfect excuse to turn “one day I should build my own profiler” into “apparently I now have strong opinions about JVM bytecode.”
The Semeru Connection
I could select one method, a class or a family of classes using wildcards.
I could exclude noisy methods.
I could trace application code and JDK classes.
I could activate actions only when a particular method was reached.
OpenJ9 even supports trigger actions such as capturing a stack trace, taking a dump, suspending tracing or resuming it around a selected execution window.
That’s exactly the kind of visibility I often miss while debugging Spark locally.
-Xtrace could reveal activity hidden beneath Spark’s public metrics, inside ordinary Java methods, constructors and library code.
No application changes.
No custom Spark build.
Just point the scanner at the suspicious part of the volcano—and, naturally, replace the JVM with IBM Semeru first.
Even that was not entirely plug-and-play.
Getting the experiment to run with Spark 3.5 exposed a Hadoop compatibility issue, so I had to make a small change to one of its classes before everything worked.
Apparently, even borrowing somebody else’s volcano requires a little home renovation.
That was the practical limitation. -Xtrace is an OpenJ9 capability, while my everyday Spark experiments never run on IBM Semeru or another OpenJ9-based runtime.
Quite often, Spark is sitting on HotSpot, where politely requesting -Xtrace achieves roughly the same result as asking a toaster for a thread dump.
Please do not test either assumption.
OpenJ9’s tracing engine lives inside the JVM and can observe native VM tracepoints.
MadLava stands outside the engine room.
It watches selected behaviour by transforming Java bytecode and injecting small reporting calls into the application.
The ideas I wanted to preserve were selective matching, wildcard filters, targeted observation and zero changes to the application source.

Recreating them, however, meant dealing with bytecode transformation, classloaders, constructors, exceptional exits, bounded metric stores and several creative new ways to make the JVM extremely unhappy.
In other words, exactly the kind of dangerously reasonable idea that belongs in an OpenAI Build Week hackathon.
The Web UI shows jobs, stages, tasks, executors, storage usage, shuffle activity, garbage-collection time, task deserialization time and result serialization time.

Classloaders do not Share your Optimism
Injecting a call to MadLavaHooks.methodEnter() is only useful if the transformed class can actually see MadLavaHooks.
That sounds obvious until multiple classloaders enter the room.
The agent classes are normally loaded by the system classloader.
Spark applications, plugins, application servers and framework internals may use other loaders.
JDK classes can be loaded by the bootstrap loader, whose worldview does not naturally include random classes from an agent JAR.
A transformer can therefore produce technically valid bytecode that references a class unavailable to the classloader defining the transformed class.

The instrumentation API provides mechanisms for adding supporting JARs to the bootstrap or system classloader search paths, but those supporting classes must be designed with very careful dependencies.
A helper loaded by the bootstrap classloader cannot casually depend on libraries visible only to the application classloader.
This is why MadLava needed a tiny runtime bridge: a minimal set of hook classes visible from the places where transformed code might execute.
Small hooks are not just a performance optimization.
They are a diplomatic agreement between classloaders.
Modules Added Another Border Checkpoint
Since Java 9, classes also belong to modules.
The instrumentation API passes the module containing the transformed class to the transformer, and Java provides facilities for expanding module readability, exports and opens where necessary.

The JVM also grants some readability support for transformed classes calling agent helper classes from unnamed modules, but named-module boundaries still require deliberate handling when deeper access is needed.
For JDK internals or strongly encapsulated named modules, it can become the difference between “successfully instrumented” and “welcome to IllegalAccessError.”
📌 This reinforced an important scope rule: MadLava should instrument only what the investigation needs.
Retransformation is not Time Travel
Registering a transformer with retransformation support doesn’t grant unlimited power over classes that have already been loaded.
First, the JVM must report that retransformation is supported.
The agent JAR must also request that capability through its manifest, and the transformer must be registered as retransformation-capable.
Even then, retransformation can modify method bodies, constant-pool entries and certain attributes, but it cannot freely reshape an existing class.
It cannot simply add or remove methods and fields, change method signatures, alter inheritance or rewrite several structural attributes as if the class had never been loaded.
For MadLava, that meant instrumentation had to be additive and structurally conservative.
Retransformation is closer to renovating an occupied apartment than rebuilding the building.
The walls may move a little.
Adding another floor is discouraged.

MadLava needed stronger rules:
Never instrument MadLava’s own hooks and collectors.

The -javaagent mechanism provided exactly the external workflow I wanted.

Which meant the next challenge was not how to inject one probe.
It was how to organize the entire agent so that thousands of probes, collectors and report updates didn’t become one enormous molten dependency graph.
A profiler touches several dangerous areas at once: JVM startup, configuration, class loading, bytecode, application threads, concurrent data structures, file output and shutdown.
Combining all of that into one heroic component would make the agent easy to start, difficult to test and almost impossible to trust.
The architecture therefore followed one basic rule: Each layer should know as little as possible about the layer after it.
The transformer shouldn’t know how JSON is written.
The output writer shouldn’t know how a method was instrumented.
The application hook shouldn’t know whether the event came from Spark, Hadoop or somebody’s surprisingly complicated getter.

At bytecode level, Java uses the ATHROW instruction to throw a Throwable.
But an ATHROW inside a method doesn’t necessarily mean the method itself failed.
The JVM first searches the current method for a compatible exception handler.

Instrument every ATHROW as a method failure and the report lies.

Another could be created as a wrapper around an existing exception, producing one new construction and a separate throw operation.

The profiler cannot infer that all constructions are bad.
It can reveal that they’re happening often enough to deserve an experiment.
Serialization / Deserialization: Observable Borders, Slippery Bytes
Serialization looked straightforward in this first specification: count objects, measure time, count bytes, go home early.
Java serialization then reminded me that an object is rarely travelling alone.
ObjectOutputStream doesn’t simply convert one isolated object into one isolated byte array.

It traverses the graph reachable from the root object, maintains stream state and remembers objects that have already been written so later references can be represented as back-references rather than complete copies.
The Java serialization specification explicitly describes ObjectOutputStream as maintaining the set of objects already serialized.

MadLava can reliably observe the boundaries that matter: when top-level serialization or deserialization starts, whether it succeeds, how long it takes and which root or resolved classes are involved.
That’s enough to reveal which classes dominate, where time accumulates, where failures cluster and whether deserialization is happening far more often than expected.
What MadLava cannot portably promise is the exact serialized size of every arbitrary root object.
The output stream may emit class metadata, headers, handles, back-references and custom writeObject data.
It may then pass those bytes through buffering or compression before they reach the underlying destination.
The serialized form represents an object graph and stream history, not a neat invoice attached to one Java instance.
Java’s serialization protocol has explicit representations for new objects, classes, arrays, strings and references to objects already present in the stream.

Now add: buffered streams, custom serializers, shared references, stream resets, compression, nested serialization calls, objects that implement their own writeObject, several layers observing the same physical write.
At that point, claiming “this object was exactly 8,417 bytes” becomes less profiling and more creative accounting.
MadLava therefore reports root-operation counts and timing while marking exact portable byte attribution as unavailable where it cannot be established honestly.
The result is not a heap census.
It’s not a complete inventory of every nested class Spark touched while serializing a closure.
And it’s definitely not permission to add every byte counter from every stream layer and announce that Spark serialized the moon.
It’s targeted evidence around observable serialization boundaries.
Deserialization Creates Objects without Asking their Constructors
Deserialization introduces another useful distinction.
For ordinary Java code, object construction usually involves allocation followed by a constructor invocation.
During standard Java deserialization, however, constructors and field initializers of serializable classes are not executed.
The object’s memory is allocated, its fields begin with default values, and its serialized state is restored
only the first non-serializable superclass constructor is invoked.
This means constructor-based instance tracking and deserialization tracking observe different realities.
An object restored from an ObjectInputStream may exist without appearing in the normal constructor count for its serializable class.
That’s not a lost event caused by a lazy profiler.
That’s how Java serialization works.
It also explains why MadLava keeps serialization visibility separate from general object-construction counts.
Combining them would produce a cleaner diagram and a dirtier meaning.

As already discussed, deserialization can allocate serializable objects without invoking their constructors.

ATHROW does not Necessarily Mean the Method Failed
The JVM uses ATHROW to throw a Throwable, but executing ATHROW does not automatically mean that the current method exits exceptionally.
The JVM first searches for a matching handler inside the same method.
Only when no local handler catches the exception does the method complete abruptly.
Counting every observed ATHROW as a failed invocation would report an error even though the caller received a perfectly ordinary zero.
So the transformation cannot simply inject:

The catch-all handler observes only exceptions that would otherwise leave the method.
It then rethrows the same Throwable, preserving the application’s behaviour.
MadLava must not replace the exception.
It must not wrap it.
It must not modify its message.
It must not accidentally catch it and forget to throw it again because the metric update looked more important at the time.
📌 A profiler should observe exceptional control flow, not provide an alternative ending.

The report needs four clearly named measurements, not one mysterious counter called exceptions.

The bridge is not the profiler.

Modules Added a Second Visibility System
Java 9 added the module system, giving the JVM another question to ask after: Can this classloader find that class?
The new question is: Is this module permitted to read or access it?
Modern transformers receive both the classloader and the module of the class being transformed.
Java’s instrumentation contract helps agents by arranging for a transformed class’s module to read the unnamed modules used for bootstrap and system-loader instrumentation helpers.
That’s precisely what allows injected calls to ordinary bridge classes to work in many named-module scenarios.
But that assistance is not a universal backstage pass.
If an agent needs deeper access to a package that a named module doesn’t export or open, it may need to expand module relationships deliberately.
Instrumentation.redefineModule can add reads, exports and opens for modifiable modules
it can expand access, but it cannot take existing access away.
This distinction mattered during early MadLava experimentation because the first bytecode implementation used ASM classes embedded inside the JDK.
Accessing those internal packages required module adjustments.
The final architecture moved toward a shaded, relocated external ASM dependency instead, avoiding unnecessary reliance on jdk.internal implementation details.
Modules were therefore not added to the architecture diagram to make it look expensive.
They were added because Java 11, 17 and 21 genuinely enforce boundaries that didn’t exist in the Java 8 classpath universe.
Never Profile the Profiler
The first defence is mandatory exclusion.
MadLava excludes its own agent classes, bootstrap hooks and bytecode libraries regardless of how enthusiastic the user’s include pattern becomes.
That protects against indirect recursion caused by otherwise innocent JDK operations executed from inside a hook.
A profiler needs both, because the JDK contains many methods and even more surprises.
Java streams are commonly layered:
ObjectOutputStream
BufferedOutputStream
FilterOutputStream
FileOutputStream
FilterOutputStream explicitly forwards operations to an underlying stream.
ObjectOutputStream also buffers data and eventually flushes it through to its underlying stream.
One object-serialization operation.
Several writes inside ObjectOutputStream.
One 1,024-byte write to BufferedOutputStream.
One 1,024-byte write delegated to FileOutputStream.
A high-level parser calls a buffered stream.
A report should say:
"layer": "java.io.BufferedOutputStream",
"layer": "java.io.FileOutputStream",
It shouldn’t quietly combine them into:
Top-level serialization operations for object-centric analysis.
The outer application stream for API usage.
But the report must preserve the origin of every measurement.
Also, parser, serialization and stream scenarios must avoid presenting delegated activity as independent physical work.
This is another case where instrumentation can be technically correct and analytically wrong.
After enough failed transformations, it is tempting to treat JVM verification, classloaders and modules as bureaucratic obstacles standing between the engineer and a perfectly reasonable profiler.
They are not.
The verifier stops malformed bytecode from corrupting execution.
Constructor rules stop half-built objects from escaping into the application.
Classloaders preserve isolation and type identity.
Modules enforce deliberate access between components.
The awkward part is that bytecode instrumentation operates exactly where all of those safety systems meet.
For MadLava, every transformed class therefore had to behave like a small proof:
The operand stack must remain valid.
Local variables must have the expected types on every path.
Normal and exceptional exits must record the correct outcome exactly once.
Constructors must only be observed after valid initialization.
Injected hooks must be visible to the target classloader.
Module access must be sufficient.
The profiler must never instrument itself into recursive collapse.
Layered I/O must not be reported as separate physical work.
That’s a surprising amount of ceremony for adding a timer.
But the alternative is a profiler that works beautifully until it encounters a nested constructor, a child-first classloader, a named JDK module or one sufficiently ambitious buffered stream.
A Java agent can compile perfectly, pass every utility test and still fail the moment a real JVM loads it through -javaagent.
The manifest may be wrong.
The transformer may produce invalid bytecode.
A hook may be invisible to the target classloader.
The application may behave correctly while the report quietly invents numbers.
That only proves 184 things happened without publicly complaining.
Filter tests cover exact matches, *, ?, overloaded methods, mandatory internal exclusions and the most important precedence rule:
included && !excluded
Exclusions must always win.
Otherwise, a user can carefully exclude com.madlava.* and still end up profiling the profiler because a broader include pattern was feeling persuasive.
Aggregation tests verify counts, totals, minimums, maximums, concurrent updates and cardinality limits.
They also exercise the behaviour after a bounded map fills up: new keys must be dropped or redirected to an overflow bucket without allowing memory to grow indefinitely.
These tests are not glamorous, but they protect the semantics of every later result.
If minimumNanos occasionally remains zero because of a race condition, the profiler can produce beautiful reports with fictional statistics.
Unit-testing a matcher doesn’t prove that its transformer can produce a valid class.
For that, MadLava loads the bytecode of small purpose-built classes, transforms it directly and defines the modified class through a dedicated test classloader.

MadLava records exactly one invocation with the expected completion state.
That catches problems much faster than launching Spark for every bytecode mistake.

The Nested-constructor Regression
One especially valuable regression test came from constructor instrumentation.
A constructor may create another object while preparing arguments for super(...):
A naive transformer can see the first constructor call and incorrectly decide that Child.this is now initialized.
The resulting instrumentation may use the object too early and fail JVM verification.
The regression test loads and executes exactly that structure.
It’s small, ugly and far more valuable than a test called:
testConstructorInstrumentationWorks()
which normally means it worked for the one constructor shape the author happened to remember.
This matters because -javaagent activates behaviour that ordinary in-process tests do not reproduce faithfully.
Application classes are loaded by real classloaders.
Oracle’s instrumentation contract requires the agent JAR to declare Premain-Class
if the attribute is missing, the JVM cannot start the launch-time agent correctly.
Retransformation also depends on both JVM support and the Can-Retransform-Classes manifest capability.
These are properties of the packaged JAR, not of the source tree that produced it.
Launch the child JVM with the produced agent JAR.
The process exit code alone is not enough.
A child JVM can exit successfully while MadLava silently disables a failed transformer and writes an empty report.
That is a stable application and a failed test.
Test the Report, not Merely its Existence
An integration test shouldn’t stop after confirming that a file appeared.
It must parse the report with a real JSON parser and verify its meaning.
For Throwable construction, assert the concrete type and a minimum expected count without confusing construction with throwing.
For serialization, assert successful and failed operations, root-class attribution and elapsed timing.
For bounded metrics, deliberately exceed the configured cardinality and verify overflow counters.
Constructor tests cover successful objects, inheritance, chained constructors, nested construction before super(...) and constructors that fail before completion.
Throwable tests use several subclasses rather than assuming every failure is an Exception.
Error, checked exceptions, runtime exceptions and custom Throwable subclasses travel through similar bytecode but represent different application semantics.
Serialization tests cover successful write and read operations, custom serialization methods, shared references and exceptions thrown during serialization or deserialization.
Stream tests cover positive byte counts, zero-length operations, end-of-file and failures.
A read returning -1 is EOF, not “minus one bytes successfully transferred,” no matter how convenient that would be for the counter implementation.
Configuration tests launch the actual agent with malformed JSON, missing files, invalid types and unsupported values.
The expected result depends on the selected failure policy, but the host application must not be destroyed merely because somebody left a trailing comma.

🪞 What MadLava Does Not Know
📌 A profiling report becomes dangerous the moment it looks more certain than the measurement behind it.
MadLava can count, time, group and correlate suspicious behaviour.
It can tell me that a method ran 80,000 times, that thousands of Throwable objects were constructed and that serialization occupied an uncomfortable amount of time.
It cannot look at those numbers, adjust its tiny detective hat and announce: Case closed.
Spark did it.
MadLava produces evidence.
Interpretation remains a human responsibility, at least until the raccoon intern completes its data-science certification. 🦝+🎓= 🧑‍🔬.

Correlation is still not Causation
MadLava may observe a rise in serialization time during the same interval as a garbage-collection spike.
That’s useful.
It doesn’t prove that serialization caused the GC.
The opposite may be true: GC pauses may have increased the measured wall-clock duration of serialization calls.
Both may be consequences of a third event, such as a large closure, a sudden allocation burst or an unexpectedly ambitious collect().
Likewise, repeated Throwable construction may coincide with a slow method because both originate from invalid input.
Removing the exception may hide one symptom while leaving the underlying workload unchanged.

Serialization Terminology Matters
Serialization produces several numbers that sound interchangeable until somebody tries to add them.
A top-level serialization operation means an observed call such as serializing one root object.
A stream byte count describes bytes observed moving through one particular stream or channel layer.
A serialized root size attempts to attribute bytes to one root serialization operation.
A shallow object size covers only the storage of one object, not the objects it references.
Java’s ObjectOutputStream maintains state about objects already written.
If the same object appears again, the stream may write a handle instead of serializing the object again.
It also traverses referenced objects, writes class descriptions and supports custom replacement and writeObject behaviour.
Observed stream bytes: 12,480
Every Invoice occupies exactly 12,480 bytes.
Those bytes may include headers, metadata, referenced objects and data produced by custom serialization.
They may exclude bytes still buffered above the observed layer or reflect compression below it.
And if MadLava observes both BufferedOutputStream and FileOutputStream, the same physical bytes may appear at both boundaries.
The report must preserve the measurement layer and accuracy label instead of placing every number into one column called bytes, where nuance goes to retire.
Missing Data doesn’t Mean Nothing Happened
MadLava observes only what its enabled features, filters and event sources allow it to observe.
The target was excluded.
Reports therefore need self-observability: feature states, accuracy labels, sampling rates, transformed-class counts, dropped keys, throttling decisions and errors.
MadLava should make the difference visible:
Local mode is perfect for the investigation workflow that created MadLava.
It’s fast to start.
It uses the real Spark libraries.
It executes Catalyst, serialization, closure cleaning, scheduling and task code paths.
It makes repeatable experiments possible without first negotiating access to twelve machines and a Kubernetes namespace.
That architectural difference matters.

A local test cannot fully reproduce: executor-process loss, cross-machine network latency, network partitions, worker-node disk variation, cluster-manager resource contention, container eviction, executor startup delays, host-level CPU competition, distributed shuffle skew caused by real data placement.
Local mode can reveal that one closure is serialized repeatedly.
It cannot prove how that closure behaves when shipped to 500 executor JVMs across several hosts.
It can reproduce an exception path.
It cannot reproduce an executor disappearing halfway through the exception.
📌 Use local mode to discover and narrow the code path.
Use a representative cluster to validate the operational conclusion.
Attaching the agent to the driver JVM gives visibility into the driver.
It doesn’t magically install MadLava inside every executor process.
Spark applications on a cluster use separate executor processes, each running tasks and storing application data independently.
To inspect executor-local method calls, Throwable activity or serialization internals, the agent must also be configured on the executor JVMs.
That introduces another question: Where do all those reports go?
Version 0.1 is primarily a local and driver-focused diagnostic workflow.
It writes process-local reports
it’s not a complete distributed telemetry backend that automatically merges several hundred executor timelines into one universal truth.
That limitation is intentional.
Building the agent was already enough of an OpenAI Build Week project without quietly adding a distributed database and calling it a helper class.
Spark Connect Lives Elsewhere
MadLava 0.1 focuses on classic Spark applications.
Spark Connect separates the client application from the Spark driver.
The client builds unresolved logical plans and sends them to the server over gRPC
it doesn’t run inside the same process as the driver and cannot directly access the driver JVM.
That means attaching MadLava to a Spark Connect client observes the client process.
It doesn’t provide visibility into remote driver internals.
To observe server-side Spark execution, MadLava must run inside the Spark Connect server or driver JVM.
Version 0.1 doesn’t even attempt full client-to-server tracing or correlation—that’s a different volcano entirely.
Retransformation is Useful, not Magical
Runtime reconfiguration is more complicated.
A class that is already loaded may require retransformation, and JVM support for retransformation is optional.
The agent manifest must request the capability, the transformer must be registered appropriately and each target class must be modifiable.
Even successful retransformation is not time travel.
Active stack frames continue executing the previous bytecode.
Only new invocations use the retransformed version.
Existing instances remain unchanged, and unsupported structural modifications can cause the operation to fail.
So enabling one new method filter at runtime doesn’t guarantee that every call already in progress suddenly becomes observable.
📌 Version 0.1 keeps retransformation disabled by default and treats it as an explicit advanced operation.
Choose narrow filters
Yes, restarting Spark is inconvenient.
So is discovering that half the relevant methods were already running the old bytecode while you interpreted the report.
Thread CPU measurement depends on JVM support and may need to be enabled.
Some environments impose module or container restrictions.
Complete allocation coverage through constructor probes.
Full Spark Connect client-server correlation.

Limitations are Part of the Interface
A limitation section is not an apology.
It’s calibration.
When a report says EXACT, SAMPLED, PARTIAL, JVM_REPORTED or UNAVAILABLE, that label tells the reader how much confidence to place in the value.
When it reports dropped keys, the reader knows the ranking is incomplete.
When it says “driver JVM,” nobody assumes executor-wide coverage.
When it says “Throwable constructions,” nobody writes a presentation claiming the application failed 40,000 times.
Readers will eventually discover every limitation in a debugging tool.
The only design choice is whether they discover it in the documentation — or at 3 a.m. while investigating why the documentation lied.
📌 MadLava 0.1 doesn’t know everything.
The important part is that it should know what it doesn’t know.
